entry.title: I am in Shock. My 8 weeks transformation
entry.summary: I recently looked at my two-month progress photos from the Forty Forward program, and I was genuinely shocked. So shocked that my first instinct was not to share them. Before-and-after…
entry.content:
I recently looked at my two-month progress photos from the Forty Forward program, and I was genuinely shocked.

So shocked that my first instinct was not to share them.

Before-and-after photos can be complicated. They can be motivating, but they can also be triggering. I never want to suggest that the body on the left was bad and the body on the right is good. Both bodies are mine. Both deserve respect.

I have lived in a larger body for my entire life. I have worn everything from an XL to pants ranging between sizes 12 and 18. A size 10 on my wedding day was probably the smallest I had ever been, and if I’m being honest, I’m fairly certain I got there in an unhealthy way.

So seeing such a noticeable change after two months of strength training felt almost unbelievable. But the most important transformation is not the one you can see in the photos.

This week, my husband said something that stayed with me. He told me he has loved and been attracted to my body at every size, 20 pounds up, 20 pounds down and everywhere in between.

What he finds especially attractive right now is my commitment.

He is watching me dedicate time to myself. He sees me getting up, training, making choices with intention and keeping promises to my own body.

That is what this chapter is really about.

When I look directly at my deepest fears, I know my mother’s recent illness and stroke have forced me to confront what it was like to grow up with a very sick mom.

My mom, Carolyn, had a massive heart attack at 47 years old (4 years away from my current age). She was in a coma for three months. She developed gangrene and ultimately lost both of her legs below the knee.

I was 11.

She has been seriously unwell for most of my life. Not occasionally sick. Not minorly unwell. Her health shaped my childhood and, in ways I am still understanding, shaped me.

Yesterday, my ten-year-old looked at me out of nowhere and asked, “If you had three wishes, what would you wish for?”

I told him that for myself, I would wish for health. For our family, health and wealth. And for the world, peace.

He thought for a moment and then asked, “If you had two extra wishes, would you wish for Bubbie to grow her legs back and not be sick right now, and also make Henry healthy?”

I was dumbfounded.

His insight, his empathy and his understanding of what our family carries broke something open in me. We cried together and had a very real conversation about things I wish a ten-year-old did not have to understand so deeply.

And suddenly, all of this became very clear.

I am not strength training because I am chasing the smallest version of myself.

I am doing this because I want to give my children a healthy mom.

I want to age with strength. I want to move well. I want to do everything reasonably within my control to care for this body while I have the opportunity.

I also think I am trying to heal the 11-year-old inside me who learned far too early that a mother’s health can change everything.

It saddens me beyond words that fear and painful family experiences have become part of my motivation. But they are not the whole story.

Love and my children motivating me. The possibility of a long, strong and full life is motivating me.

The physical changes are exciting, and I am proud of them. But what I am most proud of is my dedication. For two months, I have shown up for myself in a way I’m not sure I ever have before.

And I’m beginning to believe something I should have known all along:

No shit, I can do this.

I can become stronger without hating the body I started in. I can be proud of changing while still honouring every version of myself that got me here.

If you are standing at the beginning of your own chapter, let my story remind you that it is not too late to choose yourself.

Your body does needs to become smaller to be worthy, but because your life is worth being strong enough to live.

entry.title: No iPad November, Again!
entry.summary: We’re Doing No iPad November Again! This month, our family is putting the iPads away. Not because I think technology is evil, and definitely not because I believe I have…
entry.content:
We’re Doing No iPad November Again!

This month, our family is putting the iPads away.

Not because I think technology is evil, and definitely not because I believe I have parenting figured out. I have four kids. Sometimes an iPad is the reason I can make dinner, answer an email or hear myself think.

But last November, we tried going without them for a month, and the change in our house was impossible to ignore.

At first, I expected constant complaining. Instead, they barely missed them.

They played differently. They started reading. They listened to music, and one of them proudly announced, “Music is my new iPad.” They went to bed earlier, had fewer emotional outbursts and somehow became kinder and funnier. Their teachers even noticed an improvement in their reading fluency.

And they cuddled us more.

It honestly felt like we got our kids back.

I don’t think the iPads were turning them into bad kids. I think they were filling every quiet moment before boredom had the chance to become imagination, conversation or connection.

So we’re doing it again.

I know it won’t be perfect. There will be complaining, long afternoons and moments when handing over a screen would make my life much easier. This is not a moral stance or a judgment of how anyone else manages their household. It is simply a reset our family needs.

For one month, we’re making a little more room for boredom. For books. For music. For fighting over toys, figuring it out and playing together again.

Mostly, we’re making more room for each other.

I’ll let you know how it goes.

XO,
Alana

entry.title: I’m outgrowing my own story.
entry.summary: I’ve been having a hard time showing up on social media. That is a strange thing for me to admit because, for almost ten years, sharing has come naturally to…
entry.content:
I’ve been having a hard time showing up on social media.

That is a strange thing for me to admit because, for almost ten years, sharing has come naturally to me. I have let people into my businesses, my motherhood, my marriage and some of the hardest parts of my life.

I built The Mom Halo because I needed a place where mothers could be honest. Connection over perfection. For years, I knew exactly why I was showing up.

Lately, I open Instagram and don’t know what to say.

I know how to make content. I know how to write a hook, make a Reel and package something so people will respond to it. I just don’t know if I want to create something simply because I know it will perform.

I only want to share things that feel true and useful. Things that might actually help someone I care about. Oddly, wanting my work to matter more has made it harder to make anything at all.

I keep thinking about the difference between reach and impact. I don’t want to stay visible just for the sake of staying visible. I want to understand what I can genuinely offer women and where my voice can do the most good.

For a long time, motherhood was the main character of my story. It changed me, built The Mom Halo and connected me to thousands of women.

But I’m starting to wonder whether the motherhood main character is ready to take a step to the side.

Maybe she isn’t retiring completely but she just doesn’t have to carry the entire story anymore.

I feel like I have reached a new summit. I can see everything I climbed to get here, but I’m not certain the next part of the path looks the same.

I’ve been asking myself some uncomfortable questions:

If I weren’t afraid, what would I do?

If every decision were truly my own, what would I choose?

What is my actual gift?

And if I already had the life I say I want, what would an ordinary Tuesday look like?

I don’t have the answers yet.

Maybe I don’t want to quit, i’m simply tired of performing a version of myself that no longer feels complete.

So if I have seemed quieter, that is why. I’m thinking carefully about what deserves my voice and how I want to move through this next chapter.

I’m not disappearing. I’m listening.

And whatever comes next, I want it to be honest.

XO,
Alana

entry.title: If every decision I made were truly my own, what would I choose?
entry.summary: Lately, I have been thinking about the questions we ask ourselves when the life we built no longer fits quite the way it once did. There is a particular kind…
entry.content:
Lately, I have been thinking about the questions we ask ourselves when the life we built no longer fits quite the way it once did.

There is a particular kind of pressure that comes with being the person responsible for making payroll. People see the business, the flexibility and the success. They do not always see the nights spent doing the math, carrying the livelihoods of other people and wondering how long you can keep holding it all.

Sometimes, if I am being completely honest, I want to burn the whole thing down.

Not because I don’t love what I have built. I do. But I have started wondering how much of it I am still consciously choosing.

I recently read two essays from Brianna Wiest’s 101 Essays That Will Change the Way You Think. One asks us to imagine what the life we want would look like on an ordinary day. The other reminds us that our lives are not one continuous story we are required to keep following. We are allowed to close a chapter, change the plot and become someone new.

Those ideas left me with some uncomfortable questions:

If every decision I made were truly my own, what would I choose?

Not the decision that looks impressive. Not the one that makes the most sense to everyone else. Not what a successful woman, responsible mother or ambitious business owner should do.

Would I keep growing the business? Make it smaller? Change the offer? Build a bigger team? Release parts of it? Work less? Earn differently? Begin again?

And if I already had the life I say I want, what would an ordinary Tuesday actually look like?

What time would I wake up? How would I feel in my body? Who would receive my energy? What would I work on? What would I finally stop doing?

Maybe wanting to burn it all down does not mean we want to quit. Maybe it means a part of us is asking whether the life we created still belongs to us.

We do not have to reject everything we have built to choose differently. We can be grateful for the chapter that brought us here without forcing ourselves to remain in it forever.

So this is the question I am sitting with:

What would my life and business look like if I stopped making decisions based on what I should do and started choosing what feels truly mine?

What is your truth? Respond to this email, I really wanna know.

With love,
Alana

entry.title: Why my fitness has suddenly taken centre stage.
entry.summary: If you’ve noticed me talking more about fitness lately, there is a reason. And I haven’t quite known how to tell you. In the middle of July, ten days after…
entry.content:
If you’ve noticed me talking more about fitness lately, there is a reason. And I haven’t quite known how to tell you.

In the middle of July, ten days after her 80th birthday, my mom had a severe stroke.

My mom, Carolyn, is sunshine. If you know her, you know. She is our queen, our matriarch, the woman everyone wants to sit beside. She loves, gives, helps and serves. She is beautiful and gracious, but also the coolest and the most fun. The kind of mom, bubbie and mother-in-law you feel incredibly lucky to have.

And suddenly, we were in the ICU, wondering whether we would get to keep her.

This wasn’t the first time.

When my mom was 48, she had a devastating heart attack. She nearly died, and the complications resulted in her losing both legs below the knee. I was ten years old.

For the next 32 years, she lived the fullest life. Truly. She has a zest that makes you want to be near her. She has dealt with so much illness, so many physical limitations, and still made room for other people, for fun, for beauty, for joy.

Then came this summer.

She is home now, slowly recovering, and needs care 24 hours a day. So much of the mom I know is still there. But her ability to move and do things for herself has changed enormously. Watching her want to do things her body cannot currently manage is heartbreaking.

I am hopeful. I am also scared.

Right now, we’re paying attention to what brings her pleasure. What makes her smile. How she can still give love and receive it. Those moments matter so much when so much else has been taken out of your hands.

And somewhere in all of this, I started looking at my own body differently.

I am now only about five years younger than my mom was when her life first changed so dramatically. Growing up, our almost 40-year age gap felt enormous. Now, 48 feels very close.

That realization hit me hard.

I want to enter the next decades with as much strength and mobility as I can build. If I ever need to recover from an illness or injury, I want to give myself the strongest starting point I can.

I know I cannot exercise my way into a guarantee. My mom’s health challenges were never a failure of effort or spirit. But watching what recovery asks of her has made me take my own health seriously in a way I hadn’t before.

So I am making time. Moving my body. Paying attention to how I feed it. Following through even when life is full and there are a hundred other things asking for me.

Yes, I want to look better. I’m enjoying feeling better, too. I’m allowed to want that.

But when I think about why I’m doing this, I think about being able to get up, go out, join in. I think about my children getting older and the life I still want to share with them. I think about having the strength to keep doing the things that bring me pleasure.

My mom has taught me so much about living joyfully in a body that has been through hell. This summer has also taught me how much I want to care for mine while I have the opportunity.

So if you see me sharing my journey to “shred,” this is what’s underneath it.

I’m in this for the long haul. I want a full life, and I want to be as physically able to enjoy it as I can.

With love,
Alana

entry.title: Time for some truth on my daughters birthday.
entry.summary: Here is the truth: I am scared of my daughter getting older. Essa turns eight tomorrow. My only daughter, with three brothers, she holds a golden spot in my heart.
entry.content:
Here is the truth: I am scared of my daughter getting older.

Essa turns eight tomorrow. My only daughter, with three brothers, she holds a golden spot in my heart. And this birthday is hitting both of us harder than I expected.

This week, she came to me weeping.

“Mommy, I don’t want to get older. I want to stay seven forever.”

Then she said, “I already miss my childhood.”

That left me in puddles. Because I miss it too, even though we are right in the middle of it. I’m already yearning for moments that are still happening. She is here, wanting me, telling me things, asking me to come and watch. And somehow I’m missing her already.

She feels big. She loves big. She thinks big. Sometimes I hear what’s going on in that little head of hers and forget that she is still only seven.

I wonder if part of my fear is knowing some of the hardness that comes with being a girl, and then a woman. I don’t know how much of that she senses. But when she tells me she already misses her childhood, I want to pull her close and tell her there is still so much of it left.

There are monkey bars to hang from. Cartwheels to practise. New hobbies to try, get completely obsessed with, and maybe abandon a month later. She has time. I want her to feel that.

I daydream about her future, of course. I wonder who she will become and what she will love. But I know she will surprise me. She already does.

So I’m trying to meet her where she is today.

She wants to sing, dance and act? Okay, let’s go. She wants to make videos and dreams of a YouTube channel? Let’s figure it out together. She wants to spend the weekend hunting for squishies? I’m driving.

These things matter to her. I want to give them room, and I want to be there while she discovers what she likes.

For as long as she wants to roll with me, I am happily coming along. Her number one fan, her driver, the person she can ask to watch something “one more time.”

I know the tween years are coming. I know we won’t always be this easy together, and there will be days when she wants space from me. I hope I can give her that without making her responsible for how much I miss her.

But tonight, she is seven. Tomorrow, she will be eight.

I’m so proud of the girl she is becoming. I’m also having a hard time letting go of seven. Both are true, and I needed to say it.

Happy birthday, my sweet girl. There is still so much childhood ahead of you. And I’m here for all of it.
